comparison: Both strongly support the prevalence and quantitative characterization of movie-tuned neurons across brain regions (C1, C2, C23-C32). OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor and control analyses (C35, C38, C40, C41), while peer reviewers explicitly affirmed findings as 'convincing' and noted improvements after behavioral state controls. Peer review also includes C90-C91 (comparison to place cells across species), which OpenEval addresses separately in R11.

Both strongly support the persistence of movie tuning across behavioral states with appropriate controls (C3, C35, C39-C41). OpenEval emphasizes multiple independent control analyses, while peer reviewers explicitly praised these controls as making findings 'substantially more convincing.' Both reference the place cell comparison (C36), though OpenEval includes additional claims not mentioned by peer reviewers (C33, C34).

Perfect agreement on movie-field properties (C4, C5, C44-C46). Both support the quantitative characterization and statistical comparisons across brain regions. OpenEval provides detailed statistical values, while peer reviewers accepted these findings without challenge, noting comprehensive characterization as a strength.

Strong agreement on mega-scale encoding phenomenon (C6, C47-C56). Both support the extensive quantitative characterization and comparisons to place cells. OpenEval includes control analyses ruling out unit isolation artifacts (C105, C106), while peer review includes C96 (multi-scale comparison), which OpenEval addresses in R12. Both treat this as a novel and important discovery.

Both support the organizing principle of consistent cumulative duration despite variable field durations (C7, C57, C58). OpenEval provides detailed statistical comparisons, while peer reviewers accepted this finding without challenge as part of comprehensive movie-field characterization. OpenEval includes C59, not explicitly mentioned in peer review.

Strong agreement on sequence-dependent hippocampal encoding demonstrated by scrambled movie experiment (C8-C10, C72-C76, C88). Both treat this as key evidence distinguishing episodic encoding from visual feature processing. Peer reviewers called it 'a powerful method,' while OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor. OpenEval includes additional claims (C70, C71, C77, C81, C82) that peer review addresses partially in R7. Peer review includes C102 (hierarchical interpretation), which OpenEval addresses in R12.

OpenEval supports the characterization of neurons with brief, temporally precise responses (C60-C62), noting this exists even in hippocampus. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these claims, though the overall finding of diverse response properties was not challenged.

Perfect agreement on population-level analyses (C63-C69). Both support these findings as consistent with single-neuron results and the differential encoding hypothesis. OpenEval provides detailed methodological assessment, while peer reviewers accepted these as supporting evidence without raising concerns.

Strong agreement on mechanistic insights from rearrangement analysis and latency hierarchy (C78-C82). Both support the distinction between visual feature encoding and hippocampal sequence encoding. Peer reviewers accepted the latency analysis with noted exceptions to hierarchical order, while OpenEval emphasizes methodological soundness and anatomical consistency.

Both support the decoding analyses (C83-C86) demonstrating differential performance on scrambled sequences across regions. OpenEval emphasizes methodological rigor (leave-one-out cross-validation, controlled sample sizes), while peer reviewers treated these results as consistent with main findings without challenge. OpenEval includes C87, not explicitly mentioned in peer review.

Both support contextualization within broader literature (C90-C95). OpenEval emphasizes appropriate citations and qualifications, while peer reviewers affirmed the study 'bridges the gap between hippocampal rodent and human studies.' Overlap on C92-C95 (human studies connections), with OpenEval also addressing C90-C91 (place cell comparisons across species), which peer review includes in R1.

Both support the hierarchical framework with qualifications (C96-C98, C100-C101). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with acknowledged exceptions, while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, noting 'cortical processing did not quite follow an apparent hierarchical order.' Both recognize the pattern exists but has deviations (e.g., V1 vs. LGN, CA3 properties).

Both rate as UNCERTAIN regarding chunking/binding mechanisms and episodic memory claims (C103, C104, C116, C117). OpenEval notes C103 is explicitly speculative and would require additional experiments. Peer reviewers note the Discussion 'draws a clearer distinction' between visual scene representation and episodic memory encoding, indicating these interpretations are speculative rather than directly demonstrated.

Both support the distinction between movie-fields and place-fields (C105-C112). OpenEval emphasizes systematic arguments and control analyses, while peer reviewers implicitly accepted this through positive assessment of hippocampal visual encoding as distinct from spatial navigation. Peer review also includes C113-C114 (comparison to moving bar study), which OpenEval addresses in R15.

Both address unit isolation controls (C105, C106). OpenEval includes these as part of systematic arguments distinguishing movie-fields from place-fields (R14), while peer reviewers implicitly accepted data quality by not raising concerns and noting 'additional metrics applied substantiate the results.'

Partial overlap on distinguishing current findings from prior work (C113, C114). OpenEval supports the distinction from moving bar study and notes lack of response to simple stimuli (C115), treating sequence coding connection as appropriately cited but episodic memory role as speculative (C116, C117). Peer review focuses on movie-fields vs. place-fields distinction without specifically addressing the moving bar comparison.

Partial overlap on episodic memory interpretation (C116, C117). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED for distinguishing from prior work but notes episodic memory role is 'explicitly speculative.' Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, noting the Discussion clarifies hippocampal neurons were 'more likely' representing visual scenes rather than encoding episodic memory contents.

OpenEval supports the methodological details and use of publicly available dataset (C20-C22, C121-C127), noting this enhances reproducibility. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these methodological claims, though data quality was implicitly accepted.

OpenEval supports the literature review and motivation (C11-C19) as accurate with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these background claims, though the overall motivation was implicitly accepted.

Both address comparison between movie and classic stimuli (C26). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to methodological differences in presentation parameters that may confound direct comparison. Peer reviewers accepted this comparison without challenge (SUPPORTED), treating it as consistent with the hypothesis that hippocampal neurons require continuous sequences. Peer review also includes C115 (lack of response to simple stimuli), which OpenEval addresses in R15.

Perfect agreement on broader implications and significance (C89, C118-C120). Both support these conclusions as well-founded and appropriately qualified. Peer reviewers explicitly affirmed the study 'bridges the gap between hippocampal rodent and human studies' and 'should be of interest' to multiple research communities.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN the claim that non-LGN inputs contribute significantly to V1 movie tuning (C99), noting this is speculative and not directly tested. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing this claim about the V1-LGN paradox.

Peer reviewers implicitly accepted spike sorting quality and unit isolation controls (C37, C105, C106) by not raising data quality concerns. OpenEval addresses C105-C106 in R14 as part of arguments distinguishing movie-fields from place-fields, but C37 (spike sorting quality) is not explicitly evaluated by OpenEval as a standalone claim.

Peer reviewers accepted comparisons to classic stimuli and lack of response to simple stimuli (C26, C115) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval addresses C26 separately in R18 as UNCERTAIN due to methodological confounds, and C115 in R15 as part of distinguishing from prior work (SUPPORTED).
